name: FreeDOS
summary: Free and open-source operating system compatible with the MS-DOS standard for x86 computers, equipped with the DOS-C kernel, the FreeCOM shell, FAT32 support and the FDIMPLES package manager.
license: Open Source (GNU GPLv2 with various free utilities)

content.introduction: FreeDOS is a complete free and open-source operating system guaranteeing upwards software compatibility with the MS-DOS standard of IBM and Microsoft. Founded in 1994 by Jim Hall in reaction to the announced abandonment of stand-alone DOS in favour of Windows 95, FreeDOS makes it possible to run thousands of heritage software programs, to bring historical PC video games back to life and to ensure the control of industrial systems or low-level maintenance tools.
content.what_is_it: Technically, FreeDOS is a single-tasking operating system operating in 16-bit real mode on Intel x86 architecture microprocessors (from the original 8086 processor up to modern multi-core chips in legacy BIOS compatibility mode). It implements no memory isolation or distinction between user space and privileged space, granting each program direct and unmediated access to the physical hardware, the processor registers and the BIOS software interrupts.
content.kernel_architecture_and_dos_c: The heart of the system rests on the FreeDOS kernel, stemming from the DOS-C project written in the C language by Pat Villani and enriched by Bart Oldeman. This kernel faithfully reproduces the DOS interrupt vector table, in particular the famous `INT 21h` interrupt which governs input/output operations, process creation and conventional memory allocation (the first 640 kilobytes). Thanks to a modular and open structure, the kernel ensures almost perfect compatibility with the historical system calls of MS-DOS 6.22 and PC-DOS.
content.filesystems_fat32_and_memory_managers: While preserving the traditional DOS model, FreeDOS introduces major technological advances. It natively supports the FAT32 file system in addition to the historical FAT12 and FAT16 formats, making it possible to create and handle modern hard disk partitions reaching 2 TB thanks to LBA (Logical Block Addressing). The `DOSLFN` driver provides long file name management, while access to memory beyond 1 MB is handled by high-performance managers: `HIMEMX` for extended memory (XMS) and `JEMM386` for paged memory (EMS), upper memory blocks (UMB) and interrupt virtualisation.
content.shell_freecom_and_fdimples_packaging: The default textual user interface is animated by the FreeCOM command interpreter, the free successor of `COMMAND.COM`. FreeCOM brings modern comfort with a command history recallable with the arrow keys, automatic file name completion with the tabulation key and commands inspired by Unix (`grep`, `head`, `tee`, `less`, `cal`). Installation and maintenance of software are carried out by means of the interactive **FDIMPLES** manager (FreeDOS Installer - My Package List Editor Software), which organises the programs into modular categories (development, Cutemouse mouse drivers, Sound Blaster sound, games, `FDNPKG` network utilities).
content.contemporary_roles_and_virtualization: In the contemporary ecosystem, FreeDOS fulfils three major missions: retrogaming (native execution of flagship titles of the 1980s and 1990s without heavy software emulation), industrial control and embedded systems (machine tools, measurement controllers running on legacy x86 hardware), and firmware maintenance (flashing of BIOS of motherboards or RAID controllers by large manufacturers such as Dell, HP or Lenovo). On recent computers deprived of a legacy BIOS (strict UEFI without CSM), FreeDOS runs transparently within emulators such as DOSBox-X, QEMU, VirtualBox or VMware.
advantages: Software and binary compatibility with the historical MS-DOS software library.
Native support for the FAT32 file system and LBA addressing for modern hard disks up to 2 TB.
Fully free and open-source system under GNU GPL licence, without dependence on closed commercial publishers.
Negligible hardware consumption, able to run on any x86 processor with only 640 KB of RAM.
Modern FreeCOM interpreter equipped with command history, tabulation completion and Unix utilities.
Interactive FDIMPLES package manager facilitating the installation and removal of modular components.
disadvantages: 16-bit real-mode single-tasking operating system devoid of protected memory, user accounts or access rights.
Native incompatibility with strict UEFI secure boot (requires legacy CSM mode or an emulator on modern PCs).
Limited network and multimedia support, requiring specialised drivers (NDIS packet stacks, ISA/PCI sound card drivers).
Absence of 3D hardware acceleration or modern display management beyond the VGA and VESA standards and the resolutions of the period.
The crash of a single application generally causes the complete freezing of the machine, requiring a physical restart.
who_is_it_for: Retrogaming enthusiasts wishing to play classic DOS games under authentic execution conditions on real or emulated hardware.
IT technicians and repairers needing a minimalist bootable system to flash BIOS and hardware firmware.
Industrial engineers and technicians maintaining production equipment in service (CNC, controllers) driven by DOS software.
Students and the curious wishing to explore the intimate architecture of x86 hardware and the operation of low-level BIOS interrupts.
who_is_it_not_for: Users looking for a contemporary desktop system to browse the modern web, watch streaming videos or perform advanced office work.
Developers designing multi-threaded software applications or modern network microservices.
Users requiring data security, disk encryption and strict process isolation.
Multi-user server infrastructures requiring high availability and simultaneous connections.
content.verdict: FreeDOS is a complete, free and compatible reimplementation of the MS-DOS environment for processors of the x86 family. Designed on the initiative of Jim Hall to preserve access to historical 16-bit software, it brings modern support for FAT32 file systems, an enriched command interpreter (FreeCOM) and a package manager (FDIMPLES). It remains in use for running heritage industrial applications, updating firmware on motherboards and emulating historical video games.
